title: Checking Load Calculations for a Residential Renovation
problem: A homeowner wanted to remove a load-bearing wall to create an open-plan kitchen. The contractor needed structural drawings and an engineer's stamp before the city would issue a permit.
description: Marcus walks through the process of evaluating whether a load-bearing wall can be removed, calculating the required beam size to replace it, and producing the stamped drawings the city requires for a building permit.
process: Visited the site and measured the existing structure — wall dimensions, span, floor-to-ceiling height.
Reviewed the original building plans from the city's records office. They were from 1978 and partially illegible.
Identified the load path: the wall was carrying roof loads and a portion of the second-floor joists.
Calculated the tributary area and determined the total load the replacement beam would need to carry.
Sized the beam using the National Design Specification for Wood Construction tables — ended up specifying a laminated veneer lumber (LVL) beam.
Checked the bearing points at each end of the beam. One end landed on the foundation. The other needed a new post carried down to a footing.
Drew up the structural details in AutoCAD and wrote the engineering letter.
Reviewed the final package, stamped the drawings, and sent them to the contractor for permit submission.
result: Permit was approved on first submission. The contractor installed the beam and the renovation was completed without structural issues.
